Have you read The Concept of Anxiety, 1844 (!), and The Sickness Unto Death, 1849 (!)?
You are kind enough to ask whether there are any books that interest me.

My interest is very great. For example, I am looking—because of its title—for Lavelle’s La présence totale (Total Presence), published in 1930, I think. Then James Burnham, The Managerial Revolution, unless it merely repeats what we had already discovered in 1920–30. And also anything at all, book or pamphlet, by R. Capitant published after 1938.
Bernanos’s pronouncements no longer interest me.
(Mrs Schmitt asks whether the letter of August 1947 for Mrs Linn arrived, and also a small September gift—a little piece of Venetian lace .)
We in twentieth-century Europe know boastful figures of a very different order from the <…> types of the nineteenth century.
I have defied the escapades of fate.
I have looked death by the executioner’s hand in the face.
Three times I sat in the belly of the fish.
I have tasted defeat in civil war.
Changes of regime and burst water pipes.
I was discriminated against, defamed, and dismantled.
Terror from below and terror from above.
Terror on the ground and terror from the air.
Brown terror, red terror, and mottled terror.
I passed through all of it, and all of it passed through me.
(So sings—or rather boasts—the Walt Whitman of the twentieth century.)
But part of the superiority of the present age is precisely that such boasting must now come to an end.
All that is missing is a Rilke-style conclusion:
O happiness of the gnat that still jumps within!
Meanwhile I keep encountering the fatherly teacher of my brother Thomas Hobbes: the profound Francis Bacon.
His Sermones fideles, in the Leiden edition of 1644, have now become my devotional book.
Here are the basic political and philosophical insights from which Hobbes proceeds:
De invidia, on envy, Chapter IX, and De ira, on anger, Chapter LV, are the source of the psychology of competition.
And then: atheists as calmer citizens.
The conclusion: all the fox’s cunning and its many tricks are nothing beside the power of the one lion.
The fable of the fox and the lion.
“For a powerful and faithful friend gives more protection than countless arts and tricks,” etc.
An encounter with the grand style of German Idealism:
Again and again, the extraordinary position of Samuel Butler.
How can anyone write the intellectual history of the nineteenth century without knowing him?
How could Ernst Jünger write The Worker without knowing him?
The most intellectually superior treatment of the subject: technology and technocracy.
Irony and satire as elements of magic?
Not the irony of the great English writers.
“The servant glides by imperceptible approaches into the master.”
“Is not machinery linked with animal life in an infinite variety of ways?”
This belongs with the Leviathan as the great machine.
Man is a little man to man.
The little man becomes God to the little man.
We shall have to drink this entire series of variations down to the dregs, until today’s humanism has driven itself ad absurdum and all the way down to Acheron.
No kneeling before this heartless god of global deception.
The small human being, the parvus homo, grows still smaller. He becomes a homunculus, a little manufactured man.
The great human being, the magnus homo, grows still greater. He becomes the superman.
Homo homini homo—man is simply man to man—is the zero point of pure indifference.

In practice, that relationship cannot hold for even a second. It immediately divides again in order to create tension. It splits into polar opposites, like positively and negatively charged electrons.
Illum oportet crescere, istum autem minui.
One must increase; the other must decrease.
The magnus homo, the great man, “reaches up toward divinity.” He becomes a manufacturer.
The parvus homo, the little man, becomes “more animal than an animal.” He becomes a manufactured product.
The wolf is really still a very human category.
Compared with the manufactured products of the brave new world, the wolf is still a creature.
The true intensifications, in the direction of both good and evil, arise only with the intervention of spirit.
The most astonishing document of the abyssal depth of German Idealism:

“But if spiritual contingency, arbitrary will, goes so far as evil, even this is infinitely higher than all of nature—higher than the lawful course of the stars or the innocence of the plant—for that which goes astray in this way is still spirit.”
The most evil, lowest wickedness of the human spirit is still greater than the starry heavens and the most beautiful flower. Because what goes astray in this way is still spirit.
What a sentence for our German situation in 1944!
The generation immediately after Hegel gave its answer:

Truly, the new products created by the breakdown of this philosophy will be stronger than every attempt to restore the old Churches. They will unleash theurgic forces—forces that try to make divine powers real in the world—that will make our miserable self-righteous people on both right and left shudder, along with all those who profit from the gigantic humiliation of the German people.

Instead of the renouveau catholique, the Catholic revival that took place between 1910 and 1933 and went unnoticed by official institutions, we shall now experience a fantastic retour offensif: a counterattack by the philosophy of German Idealism, armed with myth—which in reality means armed with theurgy.
Hegel above all. He will cease to be, in theory, a museum piece preserved by academic philosophy, and in practice, a weapon monopolized by Moscow Marxism.

If Heidegger, with his acts of re-ontologizing, can produce such broad effects even in Gallia docens, teaching and learned France, what depth of effect will Konrad Weiss’s “Christian Epimetheus” have in Germany!
Werner Blischke was supposed to discover the identity of the I. K. who wrote an article on Sartre in issue no. 4 of Kurier, 6 January 1948:
The idea was to verify the immanent existentialism of the article. But the author could not be identified.
“It is a human plan to interrupt history, in order to leap out of history and arrive at a stable perfection.”
That is illuminating for understanding Marx.
Marx’s claim to be “scientific” means claiming that one can change the world without leaping out of history.
The machine is the instrument assigned to utopia. It is the weapon used to carry out the plan.
The machine differs from the tool because, within itself, it transcends the human being who operates the tool—the craftsman.
